literal: Every time Minister of Education Cui Guang saw him he would say: "Adjutant Yuan is refined and clear in bearing, leisurely and elegant in deportment—the stuff of a chief minister."
idiomatic: Whenever Cui Guang, Minister of Education, met him, he said, "Adjutant Yuan is graceful and poised—born to stand at the head of the government."

literal: " He was appointed Chief Administrator of the Andong sub-office in Xuzhou.
idiomatic: He was then made chief administrator of Xuzhou's Andong sub-office.

literal: The inspector Yuan Faseng rebelled; Xianhe fought him, was captured, and Faseng took his hand and ordered him to sit in joint punishment.
idiomatic: When Inspector Yuan Faseng rose in rebellion, Xianhe fought him, was taken, and Faseng seized his hand and bade him share the bench of the condemned.

literal: Xianhe said: "Xianhe and my elder uncle share one source but different branches—both are clans as firm as bedrock. Yet in a single morning you rebel with your territory. Before a recorder like Dong Hu, could your virtue not blush?"
idiomatic: Xianhe said, "My uncle and I spring from one root, though our lines diverge—we are both bedrock of the house. Yet in one morning you cast your land to rebellion. Faced with Dong Hu's brush, how could your honor not burn?"

literal: He would not sit.
idiomatic: He refused to sit.

literal: Faseng still wished to comfort and persuade him; Xianhe said: "I would rather die and become an evil ghost than sit as a rebel minister."
idiomatic: Faseng still tried to soothe him; Xianhe said, "I would sooner die a vengeful ghost than sit among rebel ministers."

literal: When they were about to kill him, his expression was composed.
idiomatic: When the moment of execution came, his face did not change.

literal: At the beginning of the Jianyi era he was posthumously enfeoffed as Inspector of Qin Province.
idiomatic: At the opening of the Jianyi era he was posthumously made Inspector of Qin Province.

literal: Yin Prince Tianci [6] was enfeoffed in the third year of Heping and appointed Great General Who Guards the South and Grand Commander of the Tiger Cage Garrison.
idiomatic: Prince Tianci of Ru'nan was enfeoffed in Heping year 3 [6] and named Great General Who Guards the South and grand commander of the Tiger Cage garrison.

literal: Later he became Grand Inner Palace Attendant.
idiomatic: Later he became Grand Inner Palace Attendant.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Gaozu's reign, Palace Director Hu Mohen of the Hall of the Center simplified the wealthy of the western Tiele tribes who also held military households into palace warriors, while taking bribes in great quantity and making selections unfairly.
idiomatic: Early in Gaozu's reign, Hu Mohen, Director of the Hall of the Center, culled wealthy western Tiele households with military obligations into palace guards—and took heavy bribes, choosing unfairly.

literal: The masses were enraged and killed Mohen and Xi Ling, acting commander of the Gao Ping garrison, whereupon all Tiele tribes rebelled.
idiomatic: The tribes rose in fury, killed Mohen and Xi Ling, acting commander at Gao Ping, and every Tiele division rebelled.

literal: An edict ordered Tianci and Attendant-within-the-Palace Luo Yun to supervise the armies in suppressing them.
idiomatic: The throne ordered Tianci and Luo Yun, attendant-within-the-palace, to lead the armies against them.

literal: The vanguard Tiele feigned surrender; Yun believed them. Vice-commander Yuan Fu said: "The Tiele look unsettled—there may be a plot. If we make no preparations now, we shall be trapped."
idiomatic: The Tiele vanguard pretended to submit; Yun trusted them. Vice-commander Yuan Fu said, "Their faces shift—they may turn. Without precautions we will be ambushed."

literal: Yun did not follow.
idiomatic: Yun would not listen.

literal: Several thousand Tiele light horsemen raided and killed Yun; Tianci barely escaped with his life.
idiomatic: Thousands of Tiele light horse struck and killed Yun; Tianci barely got away alive.

literal: Later he was made Great General Who Pacifies the North and Colonel Protector of the Xiongnu.
idiomatic: He was later made Great General Who Pacifies the North and Colonel Protector of the Xiongnu.

literal: He was repeatedly promoted to Grand Commander of Huaishuo Garrison, then punished for greed and cruelty—death was remitted and his offices and titles were struck.
idiomatic: He rose to grand commander of Huaishuo Garrison, then was condemned for rapacity and cruelty; execution was remitted but rank and titles were stripped.

literal: When he died, Emperor Gaozu wept at the Hall of Governance and Thought, posthumously restored his original title, buried him with princely rites, and gave the posthumous name Prince Ling.
idiomatic: At his death Gaozu wept at the Hall of Governance and Thought, restored his original title in death, buried him with princely honors, and styled him Prince Ling.

literal: His son Cheng, styled Wan'an.
idiomatic: His son Cheng, styled Wan'an.

literal: He died as Inspector of Qi Province; posthumous name Wei.
idiomatic: He died as inspector of Qi Province and was posthumously styled Wei.

literal: Cheng's son Qinghe was Inspector of East Yu Province.
idiomatic: Cheng's son Qinghe became Inspector of East Yu Province.

literal: When attacked by a general of Xiao Yan, he surrendered the city.
idiomatic: Attacked by one of Xiao Yan's generals, he surrendered the city.

literal: Yan made him Northern Route Commander-in-Chief and Prince of Wei.
idiomatic: Yan made him commander-in-chief of the northern route and Prince of Wei.

literal: When he reached Xiangcheng the court sent troops against him; at sight of them he fled.
idiomatic: He reached Xiangcheng; the court marched against him; he fled at the first wind of their banners.

literal: Yan rebuked him: "Your words run with a hundred tongues, your courage is that of a field mouse."
idiomatic: Yan scolded him: "You speak with a hundred tongues and fight with a mouse's heart."

literal: He was then banished to Hepu.
idiomatic: He was exiled to Hepu.

literal: Cheng's younger brother Fan, styled Pu'an.
idiomatic: Cheng's younger brother Fan, styled Pu'an.

literal: From Prince of the Blood he was gradually promoted to Inspector of Ying Province.
idiomatic: From prince of the blood he rose step by step to Inspector of Ying Province.

literal: Greedy and cruel by nature, the people could not bear his rule and drove him out together; Fan fled to Ping Province.
idiomatic: His greed and cruelty drove the people to rise together and expel him; Fan fled to Ping Province.

literal: Later he was made Grand Master of Splendid Happiness and Director of the Imperial Clan, enfeoffed as Baron of Dongyan.
idiomatic: Later he was made Grand Master of Splendid Happiness and Director of the Imperial Clan, enfeoffed Baron of Dongyan.

literal: He met his death at Heyin.
idiomatic: He was killed at Heyin.

literal: Tianci's fifth son Xiuyi, styled Shou'an, ranged widely in books and records and had considerable literary talent; Emperor Gaozu took note of him.
idiomatic: Tianci's fifth son Xiuyi, styled Shou'an, read widely and wrote well; Gaozu noticed him.

literal: From Prince of the Blood he was gradually promoted to Left General and Inspector of Qi Province.
idiomatic: From prince of the blood he rose to Left General and Inspector of Qi Province.

literal: Xiuyi, because Qi Province had repeatedly lost its inspectors, memorialized again and again to decline firmly.
idiomatic: Qi had lost one inspector after another; Xiuyi memorialized again and again to refuse the post.

literal: An edict said: "Length of life has its fate, fortune and misfortune lie in men—how can you heap up fear beyond measure and fail the charge of guarding the realm?"
idiomatic: The edict read, "Life's span is fated; luck rests in the living—why heap fear on fear and betray the charge to guard the realm?"

literal: Turning from misfortune toward fortune also happens in its season; you may build new offices."
idiomatic: Turning ill fortune to good has its seasons; you may build new offices."

literal: Thereupon he moved his seat of government to the eastern city.
idiomatic: He moved his administration to the eastern city.

literal: Xiuyi's government was lenient and he loved the people; in four years in the province he killed not a single man, and the common people for that reason cherished his memory.
idiomatic: Xiuyi governed gently and loved the people; in four years he executed no one, and the province mourned him when he left.

literal: He was transferred to Inspector of Qin Province.
idiomatic: He was transferred to Inspector of Qin Province.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Suzong's reign he memorialized on the commoners Xi and Yu and others, asking pardon for past faults and burial within the imperial tombs.
idiomatic: When Suzong came to the throne he memorialized for the degraded princes Xi and Yu, asking pardon and burial in the imperial necropolis.

literal: Empress Dowager Ling issued an edict: "The grace of receiving burial rests with the sovereign's intent—how may a frontier prince overstep his office and press such a petition!"
idiomatic: Empress Dowager Ling replied, "Burial is the sovereign's gift—how may a border prince overstep and plead it?"

literal: In the province he took many bribes.
idiomatic: In office he took many bribes.

literal: He was repeatedly promoted to Minister of the Masters of Writing.
idiomatic: He rose to Minister of the Masters of Writing.

literal: Once he held the scales of appointment he dealt only in bribes; every office great or small had a fixed price.
idiomatic: At the helm of appointments he sold every office; great and small posts each had their price.

literal: At that time Palace Attendant Ju Gao had an edict for prior promotion; the Shangdang commandery post was vacant and Ju sought it.
idiomatic: Palace Attendant Ju Gao had been slated for early promotion; when Shangdang commandery fell vacant, Ju asked for it.

literal: Xiuyi had privately already promised the post to another and refused Ju.
idiomatic: Xiuyi had already promised the post elsewhere and denied Ju.

literal: Ju spoke insolently; Xiuyi ordered his attendants to drag him.
idiomatic: Ju shouted abuse; Xiuyi had attendants haul him away.

literal: Ju cried to Heaven before the assembly and called out "Thief!"
idiomatic: Before the whole court Ju cried to Heaven and called him a thief.

literal: Someone asked Ju: "In broad daylight in the public hall, how can there be a thief?"
idiomatic: Someone asked Ju, "In open court at noon—where is the thief?"

literal: Ju pointed at Xiuyi and said: "The man on that seat defies the Son of Heaven's clear edict—whoever brings the most goods gets office; daylight robbery in the capital—is that not a great thief?"
idiomatic: Ju pointed at Xiuyi and said, "That man on the dais defies the Son of Heaven—richest bidder wins rank; this is open robbery in the capital—is he not the thief?"

literal: Xiuyi lost color.
idiomatic: Xiuyi's face went white.

literal: Ju went out still cursing.
idiomatic: Ju left still shouting curses.

literal: Later he wished to intercept the imperial carriage to lay out Xiuyi's crimes; Left Vice Director Xiao Baoyin persuaded him and he stopped.
idiomatic: Later he meant to waylay the imperial carriage and accuse Xiuyi; Xiao Baoyin, Left Vice Director, talked him down.

literal: When the Two Qins rebelled, Xiuyi was given concurrent appointment as Right Vice Director of the Masters of Writing, Western Route Grand Mobile Office, and acting Qin Province affairs, with command over all armies.
idiomatic: When the Two Qins rose, Xiuyi was made concurrent Right Vice Director, Western Route grand mobile office, and acting governor of Qin, commanding the armies.

literal: Xiuyi was fond of wine and drank for days on end; he then contracted wind illness, his mind clouded, and though he reached Chang'an he brought no benefit of command at all.
idiomatic: Xiuyi loved wine and drank for days; wind sickness struck, his mind dimmed, and even at Chang'an he could not command.

literal: Yuan Zhi was defeated and lost; the rebels advanced east to Blackwater; Xiao Baoyin was again sent to suppress them, with Xiuyi made Inspector of Yong Province.
idiomatic: Yuan Zhi was destroyed; rebels reached Blackwater; Baoyin was sent again, and Xiuyi made Inspector of Yong Province.

literal: He died in the province [7] and was posthumously made Minister of Works; posthumous name Wen.
idiomatic: He died in office [7], was posthumously made Minister of Works, and styled Wen.

literal: His son Jun held office as Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
idiomatic: His son Jun was Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.

literal: Prince Wanshou of Lelang was enfeoffed in the third year of Heping, appointed Great General Who Pacifies the East, and stationed at Helong.
idiomatic: Prince Wanshou of Lelang was enfeoffed in Heping year 3, made Great General Who Pacifies the East, and garrisoned Helong.

literal: Greedy and violent by nature, he was recalled and died of grief on the road.
idiomatic: Greedy and brutal, he was recalled and died of grief on the road.

literal: Posthumous name Prince Li.
idiomatic: Posthumous name: Prince Li.

literal: His son Prince Le Ping of Kang succeeded.
idiomatic: His son, Prince Le Ping of Kang, succeeded.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: His son Changming succeeded.
idiomatic: His son Changming succeeded.

literal: Punished with mandated death for murder; the state was abolished.
idiomatic: Condemned to death for murder; the fief was abolished.

literal: His son Zhong, in Emperor Suzong's time, had the former title restored and held office as Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
idiomatic: His son Zhong, under Suzong, recovered the old title and became Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.

literal: Emperor Chu boated on the Celestial Abyss Pool and ordered the princes of the imperial clan to attend the feast.
idiomatic: Emperor Chu drifted on the Celestial Abyss Pool and summoned the clan princes to feast.

literal: Zhong was stupid and without wisdom, fond of clothes by nature; he therefore wore a red gauze jacket with embroidered collar, indigo silk trousers, and brocade trim.
idiomatic: Zhong was dull and witless, mad for dress; he came in red gauze with an embroidered collar, indigo trousers, brocade hems.

literal: The emperor said: "Court dress should have a fixed form—why wear the costume of variety performers?"
idiomatic: The emperor said, "Court dress has its form—why come in acrobat's colors?"

literal: Zhong said: "What I have loved since youth lives in brocade and gauze; song-robes and dance-garments are my wish."
idiomatic: Zhong said, "Since boyhood I have loved silk and gauze; singing robes and dancing dress are all I ask."

literal: The emperor said: "For a man to be so without decency—it has come to this!"
idiomatic: The emperor said, "To lack decency so utterly—how far you have fallen!"

literal: Prince Luohou of Guangping was enfeoffed in the second year of Heping.
idiomatic: Prince Luohou of Guangping was enfeoffed in Heping year 2.

literal: He died; posthumous name Shang.
idiomatic: He died; posthumous name Shang.

literal: Having no son, later the fifth son of Prince You of Yangping, Kuang, was made his heir.
idiomatic: He had no son; later Kuang, fifth son of Prince You of Yangping, was made his heir.

literal: Kuang, styled Jianfu, was upright by nature and had spirit and integrity.
idiomatic: Kuang, styled Jianfu, was stiff-backed by nature, with spirit and backbone.

literal: Emperor Gaozu valued him [8] and said: "Uncle, you will surely give form to the altars of state and steady my person; you may now change your name to Kuang, to fulfill the beauty of seeing things through to the end."
idiomatic: Gaozu favored him [8] and said, "Uncle, you will brace the altars and steady my throne; take the name Kuang now, that you may finish what you begin."

literal: When Emperor Shizong took the throne, Kuang was repeatedly promoted to Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
idiomatic: When Shizong succeeded, Kuang rose to Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.

literal: Ru Hao first gained favor; the hundred officials slightly feared him.
idiomatic: Ru Hao first won favor; officials learned to fear him.

literal: Shizong once returned from the imperial tombs, ordered Kuang to ride beside him, and also commanded Hao to mount the carriage.
idiomatic: Returning from the tombs, Shizong set Kuang beside him and told Hao to mount the carriage too.

literal: Hao lifted his robe to ascend; Kuang remonstrated and stopped him; Shizong pushed Hao down; Hao hated Kuang and lost color.
idiomatic: Hao gathered his skirts to climb in; Kuang barred him; Shizong shoved Hao down; Hao glared, bloodless.

literal: At the time people admired his loyal bluntness.
idiomatic: Men of the time praised his blunt loyalty.

literal: When Shizong took personal rule, Kuang was made Inspector of Si Province.
idiomatic: When Shizong took the reins himself, Kuang was made Inspector of Si Province.

literal: Kuang having already offended Hao, feared harm from him, cultivated integrity and caution, and had a strong reputation for achievement.
idiomatic: Having crossed Hao, Kuang feared assassination, tightened his conduct, and won a name for clean rule.

literal: He was transferred to Inspector of Heng Province and summoned as Grand Director of the Imperial Clan and Rectifier of Henan.
idiomatic: He was moved to Heng Province, then recalled as Grand Director of the Imperial Clan and rectifier of Henan.

literal: Kuang memorialized that the wives of imperial princes and of the first- and second-rank princedoms all bore the title consort, while third-rank princedoms and below were only called wives—above they could not share the title consort, yet below they did not reach the titled ladies of fifth rank and above; he privately found this doubtful.
idiomatic: Kuang argued that first- and second-rank princes' wives were consorts, but third rank and below were merely "wives"—too low to share "consort," yet above the titled ladies of fifth rank—and asked that the rule be clarified.

literal: An edict said: "When the husband is honored at court, the wife is glorified in the chamber; a woman's standing is not fixed—she rises with her husband."
idiomatic: The edict said, "Honor the man at court and the wife shines at home; a woman's rank is not fixed—she rises with her husband."

literal: The third-rank princedoms having opened royal enfeoffment, the title consort should likewise be equal.
idiomatic: Third-rank princes now hold royal fiefs; their wives should share the title consort.

literal: Wife means equal; in principle she is equal to oneself—she may follow the consort precedent."
idiomatic: Wife means equal; in principle she stands level with her lord—let her follow the consort rule."

literal: From then on the titles of third-rank princes' wives were first fixed.
idiomatic: From then the titles of third-rank princes' wives were fixed.

literal: Later he was made Minister of Revenue.
idiomatic: Later he was made Minister of Revenue.

literal: Kuang memorialized citing the precedents of Leling and Zhangwu, asking to continue Prince Luohou's fief; the edict was referred to the Masters of Writing for deliberation.
idiomatic: Kuang cited Leling and Zhangwu and asked to revive Luohou's fief; the matter went to the Masters of Writing.

literal: The Masters of Writing memorialized permission to inherit the fief, to make clear the principle of reviving extinct lines.
idiomatic: They recommended allowing succession, to show the principle of reviving extinct lines.

literal: Kuang was at odds with Director Gao Zhao and never showed a submissive bearing.
idiomatic: Kuang clashed with Director Gao Zhao and never bowed his head.

literal: At that time Shizong entrusted government to Zhao; the court leaned in fear, and only Kuang stood against Zhao.
idiomatic: Shizong left power to Zhao; the court bent before him—only Kuang held the line.

literal: He had first built a coffin for himself and placed it in the main hall, intending to carry the coffin to the palace gates, lay out Zhao's crimes, and kill himself in desperate remonstrance.
idiomatic: He had built his own coffin and set it in the hall, meaning to haul it to the gates, denounce Zhao, and die in protest.

literal: Zhao heard of it and hated him.
idiomatic: Zhao heard and hated him for it.

literal: Later, because of disputing weights and measures with Grand Director of Imperial Sacrifices Liu Fang, he came to open quarrel with Zhao.
idiomatic: Later he quarreled with Liu Fang over weights and measures and fell into open feud with Zhao.

literal: Censor-in-Chief Wang Xian memorialized against Kuang, saying:
idiomatic: Censor-in-Chief Wang Xian accused Kuang, writing:

literal: Since the Metal Line lost the reins, many false regimes rose in rivalry; rites were broken and music collapsed, and the great norms were overturned.
idiomatic: Since Jin lost the mandate, pretenders multiplied; ritual and music shattered and the great norms fell.
